Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

We will first determine the structure forced by the condition
\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j).
\]

Taking \(i=j\) gives
\[
|A_i|=\gcd(i,i)=i.
\]
Also, if \(g=\gcd(i,j)\), then \(g\mid i,j\), so
\[
A_g\subseteq A_i\cap A_j.
\]
But \(|A_g|=g\) and \(|A_i\cap A_j|=g\), hence
\[
A_i\cap A_j=A_{\gcd(i,j)}. \tag{1}
\]

For any positive integer \(x\) that appears in some \(A_i\), let \(n(x)\) be the least index with \(x\in A_{n(x)}\). If \(x\in A_i\), then by (1),
\[
x\in A_{\gcd(n(x),i)}.
\]
By minimality of \(n(x)\), we must have \(\gcd(n(x),i)=n(x)\), so \(n(x)\mid i\). Thus \(x\) appears exactly in the sets \(A_i\) where \(n(x)\mid i\).

For each \(n\), define the block
\[
B_n=\{x:n(x)=n\}.
\]
The blocks \(B_n\) are disjoint, and
\[
A_n=\bigcup_{d\mid n} B_d.
\]
Therefore
\[
n=|A_n|=\sum_{d\mid n}|B_d|.
\]
By induction using \(\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n\), we get
\[
|B_n|=\varphi(n).
\]

So for every \(n\), there are exactly \(\varphi(n)\) elements that belong to \(A_i\) precisely when \(n\mid i\).

Now consider the divisors of \(250\):
\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250.
\]
Their \(\varphi\)-values are
\[
1,1,4,4,20,20,100,100.
\]
For \(d\mid 250\),
\[
A_d=\bigcup_{m\mid d}B_m,
\]
so
\[
\max A_d=\max_{m\mid d}(\max B_m).
\]

Let \(L_m=\max B_m\) and \(w_m=\varphi(m)\). Order the eight divisors \(m\mid 250\) by increasing \(L_m\), say \(m_1,\dots,m_8\), and let
\[
P_k=\sum_{r=1}^k w_{m_r}.
\]
The first \(k\) blocks contain \(P_k\) distinct positive integers, all at most \(L_{m_k}\), so
\[
L_{m_k}\ge P_k.
\]
Thus the desired sum is at least the minimum over all orderings of
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max_{m\mid d} p_m,
\]
where \(p_m\) is the prefix sum up to \(m\) in that ordering.

We now minimize this expression.

If \(x\mid y\) but \(y\) appears immediately before \(x\), swapping them cannot increase the expression. Indeed, if \(T\) is the sum before the pair, with weights \(a=w_x\), \(b=w_y\), then before the swap
\[
p_x=T+b+a,\qquad p_y=T+b,
\]
and after the swap
\[
p_x'=T+a,\qquad p_y'=T+a+b.
\]
For any \(d\), the maximum over divisors of \(d\) does not increase. Hence an optimal ordering may be assumed to respect divisibility: if \(x\mid y\), then \(x\) comes before \(y\).

In such an ordering, \(1\) is first and \(250\) is last. Moreover, for each \(d\mid 250\), \(d\) comes after all its proper divisors, so
\[
\max_{m\mid d}p_m=p_d.
\]
Thus we need to minimize
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}p_d.
\]

It remains to order the six intermediate divisors
\[
2,5,10,25,50,125
\]
with weights
\[
1,4,4,20,20,100
\]
and precedence constraints:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{divisor} & \text{weight} & \text{must come after}\\ \hline
2&1&-\\
5&4&-\\
10&4&2,5\\
25&20&5\\
50&20&10,25\\
125&100&25
\end{array}
\]

The optimal order is forced by simple exchange arguments:

- \(125\) has no successor among these six and has largest weight, so it should be last.
- Then \(50\) is second last, since it requires \(10\) and \(25\).
- Among \(2,5,10,25\), the job \(25\) has no successor within this group and is heavier than \(2\) and \(10\), so it should be last among them.
- Finally, \(10\) must come after \(2\) and \(5\), and putting \(2\) before \(5\) is better because the completion-time sum for \(2,5\) is \(1+5=6\) rather than \(4+5=9\).

So the optimal order is
\[
2,5,10,25,50,125.
\]
The corresponding prefix sums for all eight divisors are
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_1&=1,\\
p_2&=2,\\
p_5&=6,\\
p_{10}&=10,\\
p_{25}&=30,\\
p_{50}&=50,\\
p_{125}&=150,\\
p_{250}&=250.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the minimum possible value of the required sum is
\[
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

This value is attainable: take \(\varphi(n)\) elements in each block \(B_n\), label the blocks in the order
\[
B_1,B_2,B_5,B_{10},B_{25},B_{50},B_{125},B_{250}
\]
with consecutive positive integers starting at \(1\), and define
\[
A_i=\bigcup_{n\mid i}B_n.
\]
Then the intersection conditions hold, and the maxima for \(d\mid 250\) are exactly the values above.

Thus the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}
\]
